title: De transformatione serierum in fractiones continuas, ubi simul haec theoria non mediocriter amplificatur

deep.reconstruction:
This is the opening page of E593. Euler sets up the general simple continued fraction s = a + 1/(b + 1/(c + 1/(d + ...))) and its successive approximating fractions (convergents): A/𝔄 = a, B/𝔅 = a + 1/b, C/ℭ = a + 1/(b + 1/c), and so on. The last of these gives the true value. Clearing denominators gives A/𝔄 = a/1, B/𝔅 = (ab+1)/b and C/ℭ = (abc+a+c)/(bc+1).

In §2 he notes the key structural fact. Each convergent comes from the previous one by substituting the last partial quotient p → p + 1/q. So, in general, if P/𝔓 is built from the indices a,…,p, then Q/𝔔 comes from it by p → p+1/q, and R/ℜ comes from Q/𝔔 by q → q+1/r.

He then observes that P and 𝔓 are multilinear polynomials in a, b, …, p (no letter appears beyond the first degree). In modern terms these are continuants, numerator K(a,…,p) and denominator K(b,…,p).

§3 begins exploiting this linearity in p. Write P = M + Np and 𝔓 = 𝔐 + 𝔑p. On the next page this yields the standard three-term recurrence R = P + Qr, ℜ = 𝔓 + 𝔔r.

The page's purpose is to give a 'plain and clear' proof of the well-known convergent recurrence. That recurrence is the groundwork for the paper's real aim: converting series into continued fractions.
errors: No mathematical errors. The values (ab+1)/b and (abc+a+c)/(bc+1) are correct.
'Harum fractionum vltima verum valorem exprimet' tacitly treats the infinite case as a limit without any convergence argument. This is standard for the period.

ideas.what: Convergents of a simple continued fraction, and the substitution p → p+1/q that generates each convergent from the previous one
ideas.modern_name: Convergents; continued fraction as a composition of Möbius maps
ideas.usually_credited_to: Wallis and Huygens (17th c.); Euler, E71 (1737/1744)
ideas.where_published: E71 'De fractionibus continuis dissertatio'; Introductio in analysin infinitorum vol. I, ch. 18

ideas.what: Numerator and denominator of a convergent are multilinear (degree ≤ 1 in each index) polynomials in the partial quotients
Writing P = M + Np, linear in the last index, as a route to proving the recurrence (completed on the next page)

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely introductory, textbook material: convergents, the substitution trick, and multilinearity (continuants). All of it is well documented in Euler's earlier works and in the general literature.
transcription_corrections: §3: 'alii vero cum tanquam factorem inuoluunt' should read 'eum tanquam factorem' (the image reads 'eum'/'cum' ambiguously; 'eum' is grammatically required).
In the line D/𝔇 the image shows 'd + etc.' under c+1. This is consistent with the transcription, though the intended fourth convergent is a+1/(b+1/(c+1/d)).
